strategies.name: Current corn-soybean (no cover)
strategies.short: Keep today's rotation: the reference every other option is compared to
strategies.why: This is what most fields here do now. Satellites show these fields bare about 92% of the time from October to May. About 93% of the modelled nitrate leak falls in those months, when rain and snowmelt drain through wet soil and no living roots take up nitrate.

evidence.text: Iowa State: an average Iowa corn or soybean acre loses about 30 lb nitrate-N a year (15-50 typical; corn and soybean years are similar).

River-calibrated estimate for the Raccoon basin, 2016-2025: about 16 lb N per row-crop acre per year reaches the Van Meter gauge (range by year shown on the field card). This is what is left after losses in ditches and streams, so the loss at the field edge is likely higher.
evidence.source: Field to Faucet calibration to USGS 05484500 nitrate sensor + flow

strategies.satellite_evidence: NASA HLS (Landsat + Sentinel-2), 1,769 fields, 2020-2025: bare 92% of Oct-May and 63% of Apr-Jun. Winter living cover seen on 2.5% of field-winters 2021-2026.

yield_risk.text: No change from what you do now.

gaps: The field estimate is for a 40-acre grid square, not your surveyed field.
Your own N rate, timing, manure and tile layout are not known to the model.
risks_local_review: Doing nothing keeps fall-to-spring nitrate losses where they are, and the most loss comes in wet years like 2016-2019 and 2024-2025.

strategies.name: Cereal rye before soybean
strategies.short: Drill rye after corn harvest; end it before or at soybean planting (every other winter)
strategies.why: Living rye roots take up nitrate in the months these fields sit bare. On the average field here, 93% of the modelled leak falls October-May, and Apr-Jun gets 34% of the year's big-storm days. Rye before soybean is the lowest-risk niche: soybean yield is rarely hurt.

evidence.text: Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy (2024 science update): rye cuts nitrate-N in drainage by 28% on average, SD 26 (earlier INRS table: 31%, SD 29). Very variable: it depends on how much rye grows.
USDA-ARS 14-year tile-drainage experiment near Ames: rye cut nitrate load 57%.
Other Iowa sites: 15-48% lower nitrate with rye.
Midwest trials 2019-2021: ending rye before, at or after soybean planting did not reduce soybean yield in 27 of 28 location-years.
Over ~10 years, rye before soybean had no detectable yield effect in 20 of 29 trials and raised soybean yield in 8.
evidence.source: Practical Farmers of Iowa & Iowa Learning Farms long-term winter cereal rye cooperator study, summarized in Gailans S. (2019) 'Using Science (secondary)

strategies.satellite_evidence: HLS sees a rye-like spring green-up (NDVI >= 0.30 in mid-March to early May) on only 2.5% of field-winters here (2021-2026); 9% of fields showed it at least once. The bare window it would fill is visible on each field's leak calendar.

n_loss_reduction.source: INRS 2024 update 28% (SD 26, 2024 update); applies in the soybean years only, so a corn-soy field keeps about half of this per year on average (earlier INRS table: 31%, SD 29)

yield_risk.text: Before soybean: no yield loss in 27 of 28 Midwest location-years (2024), no detectable effect in 20 of 29 Iowa farmer strip trials and a gain in 8. Long-term adopters in a satellite study saw about 3.5% lower soybean yield, so manage termination well.

soil_health: Less erosion: rye cut interrill erosion about half and rill erosion about 90% in a central Iowa test (Kaspar 2001).
More water soaks in: cover crops raised infiltration about 35% (meta-analysis, Basche & DeLonge 2019).
Slowly more soil carbon: about +4% with grass covers (global meta-analysis, He et al. 2025).
Lower total N2O (via less nitrate leaving) in a 10-year central Iowa study (Parkin 2016).
gaps: How much rye grows on your field each year (fall seeding date, winter, spring termination date) sets most of the benefit; the trial range is wide.
Satellite cover detection misses small rye that never reaches NDVI 0.30, so true adoption may be a bit higher than shown.
Rye every winter (also before corn) roughly doubles the N kept, but corn after rye needs careful N and termination management.
risks_local_review: Termination timing and method (herbicide, roller) before or at soybean planting.
Seed availability and a seeding window right after corn harvest (drill vs. aerial).
Herbicide carryover from the corn year can hurt rye establishment.
Cash flow: seed and seeding are paid in fall, cost-share comes later.
Crop-insurance rules for cover crop termination (NRCS/RMA guidelines).

who_pays.detail: about $74/acre (FY2026 Iowa, single species, regular rate); $89/acre for historically underserved producers (secondary source; confirm before relying on it)
$30/acre first-time, $20/acre returning users, up to 160 acres
$25/acre on up to 500 acres in the 22 participating counties, stackable with the state program; check whether your county is included
$5/acre off the premium, only on acres without other cover-crop cost-share

cost_usd_ac.basis: per acre per year, averaged over the corn-soybean rotation (rye is planted every other fall); seed + custom drilling, termination pass not included
cost_usd_ac.source: ISU custom rate survey (drilling $9-25) + ISU rye seed ($15-30)

strategies.name: Extended rotation: corn-soybean-oats-alfalfa (4 years)
strategies.short: Add oats seeded with alfalfa, then a full alfalfa year, to the corn-soy rotation
strategies.why: Oats, then alfalfa, keep living roots in the soil for about two of four years, including the fall and spring months when these fields now sit bare (92% of Oct-May on average). Alfalfa also supplies N to the next corn crop, so less fertilizer is bought.

evidence.text: INRS 2024 science update: an extended rotation of 4 or more years cuts nitrate-N in drainage by 27% on average, SD 25 (earlier INRS table: 42%, SD 12). A 3-year corn-soy-small grain rotation is lower: 15% (SD 34).
ISU Marsden trial (2003-2011): 3- and 4-year rotations with far less synthetic N and herbicide had grain yields and profit similar to or greater than corn-soy.
Maize averaged 4% higher in the 3- and 4-year rotations than in corn-soy, despite far less N and herbicide.
evidence.source: Davis A.S., Hill J.D., Chase C.A., Johanns A.M., Liebman M. (2012) Increasing cropping system diversity balances productivity, profitability (full_text)

evidence.text: Soybean averaged 9% higher in the diverse rotations.
evidence.source: Davis A.S., Hill J.D., Chase C.A., Johanns A.M., Liebman M. (2012) Increasing cropping system diversity balances productivity, profitability (full_text)

strategies.satellite_evidence: HLS: alfalfa and oat/clover fields stay green from April to October and regrow in fall; in this area almost no field shows that pattern today (the fields here are corn or soybean in at least 7 of 10 years, CDL).

n_loss_reduction.source: INRS 2024 update, 4+ yr rotation 27% (SD 25, 2024 update) (earlier INRS table: 42%, SD 12)

yield_risk.text: Corn and soybean yields were similar or higher in the Marsden trial (about +4% corn, +9% soybean), but you grow oats and alfalfa two years in four, so income depends on hay and oat markets or livestock.

soil_health: Much less bought N: synthetic N use fell 80-86% in the Marsden diverse rotations (with manure).
Herbicide use fell 88% with equal weed control (Marsden).
More stable corn yields in drought: diverse rotations cut drought-year losses 14-90% across North American sites (Bowles 2020).
Can interrupt corn-soybean pest cycles (no trial number in our evidence set; ask your agronomist how much for your field).
gaps: INRS numbers come from rotations with at least 2 years of alfalfa; a 3-year version with oats/red clover is much less certain (15%, SD 34).
Local markets for oats, straw and hay, and whether livestock are nearby, are not in the model.
The Marsden profit result used manure and 2003-2011 prices.
risks_local_review: Hay equipment, storage and labor for alfalfa.
Buyer or livestock outlet for oats and hay.
Alfalfa stand termination before corn and the N credit to use.
Lease terms, base acres and crop insurance for small grains and hay.
Cash flow during the switch-over years.

who_pays.detail: payment rate not verified yet; ask your NRCS field office; CSP can also support resource-conserving rotations

cost_usd_ac.source: ISU Marsden trial: profit of the 4-yr system similar to or greater than corn-soy (2003-2011 prices, with manure); no verified $/acre for a farm switching today

strategies.name: Prairie on about 10% of the field
strategies.short: Plant native prairie strips (or retire the wettest corner) on about a tenth of the field
strategies.why: Perennial prairie has living roots all year. The INRS land-retirement (CRP) efficiency applies to the converted acres. On tile-drained ground, most tile water passes under strips, so we count only the converted area; the measured big wins are less erosion, phosphorus and runoff.

evidence.text: INRS: land retirement (CRP) cuts nitrate-N by 85% (SD 9) on the converted land; no new data in the 2024 update.
ISU STRIPS (Schulte et al. 2017): about 10% prairie in small non-tiled watersheds cut groundwater nitrate about 72% and runoff total N about 70%. Not tile drainage, so not directly comparable.
Prairie strips cut sediment export about 20-fold (~95%) versus all-crop catchments.
evidence.source: Schulte L.A., Niemi J., Helmers M.J., Liebman M., Arbuckle J.G., James D.E., Kolka R.K., O'Neal M.E., Tomer M.D., Tyndall J.C., et al. (2017 (full_text)

evidence.text: Yield per cropped acre was unchanged. Whole-catchment production fell only by the share of land taken out.
evidence.source: Schulte L.A., Niemi J., Helmers M.J., Liebman M., Arbuckle J.G., James D.E., Kolka R.K., O'Neal M.E., Tomer M.D., Tyndall J.C., et al. (2017 (full_text)

strategies.satellite_evidence: HLS would show a strip that stays green from April to November; the field leak calendar shows where the bare-and-wet months are, but a 40-acre square cannot show which part of your field is wettest.

n_loss_reduction.source: whole-field effect = 10% converted x INRS CRP 85% (SD 9); assumes the converted strip leaked like the field average

yield_risk.text: Yield on the cropped 90% was unchanged in the ISU STRIPS watersheds; you give up the crop on the strip acres (counted in the cost).

soil_health: Total phosphorus in runoff cut about 77%.
gaps: The model cannot see which 10% of a 40-acre square is the wettest or leakiest; putting prairie over a tile outlet area or wet depression may keep more N than shown.
Prairie strips are not an INRS tile-drainage practice; the nitrate number on tile-drained land is uncertain.
For tile water itself, edge-of-field practices (saturated buffers 45%, bioreactors 24% of treated drainage in the 2024 update) are the INRS options to ask about.
risks_local_review: Where strips go relative to tile lines, waterways and slope.
Establishment takes more than one season, with weed control (usually mowing) early on; ask the STRIPS team or NRCS for your site.
CRP contract length and rules (haying/grazing limits).
Lost income on the strip acres; landlord agreement if rented.

who_pays.program: USDA FSA Continuous CRP, practice CP-43 (prairie strips)
who_pays.detail: annual rental payment plus establishment cost-share on the strip acres; ISU STRIPS reports this cuts the farmer's cost by roughly three-quarters (secondary, web summary)
site design, seed mixes and cost calculator

cost_usd_ac.basis: per treated (whole-field) acre per year, mostly rent/income lost on the strip acres, before CRP payments
cost_usd_ac.source: ISU STRIPS economics ($24-35 in the 2013 study, $28-39 in the 2017 edition); secondary (web search summary, not yet in facts.json)

disclaimer: Decision support, not a replacement for your agronomist. Numbers are estimates from satellite data, weather, soils and Iowa field trials, calibrated to the rivers at Des Moines; check every option with your agronomist, NRCS or county office before changing anything.
method: Field leak (lb N/acre/yr) = satellite-seen bare ground x wet-soil drainage (NASA POWER) x soil drainage class, calibrated each year so all fields and sub-watersheds add up to the nitrate load measured by USGS at Van Meter / Des Moines. Ranges: 10th-90th percentile over 2016-2025 weather years, the calibration uncertainty and the trial range of each practice. Fertilizer value uses N price U[$0.53, $0.70]/lb N: high = USDA AMS Iowa anhydrous (secondary, https://mymarketnews.ams.usda.gov/filerepo/sites/default/files/2863/2026-04-27/1321477/ams_2863_00161.pdf, $0.668 central); low = ISU A1-88 2026 budget $0.53/lb N; it is an upper bound because the next crop does not recover all retained N. Leak and N kept are counted as nitrate that would have reached the river gauge; some nitrate is removed in ditches and streams on the way, so the N kept at the field edge is likely larger than shown.

units.lbN_kept_ac: lb N per acre per year, averaged over the rotation
